newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Clinton pushing Infotech trade plan at APEC.
newsitem.headline: Clinton pushing Infotech trade plan at APEC.

text.p: President Clinton tired Sunday to persuade fellow Asian-Pacific leaders to back a U.S. plan to free trade in computers and telecommunications by the turn of the century, a senior U.S. official said.
Clinton was to meet 17 other leaders of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum at a former U.S. military base in Subic Bay Monday to discuss a broad range of trade issues.
The leaders held an informal session Sunday.
"I'm hopeful we can see some progress," which would be reflected in the leaders' declaration following Monday's summit, said the U.S. official, who spoke on condition he not be identified.

Both Clinton and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto were expected to ask the others to support an Information Technology Agreement at next month's inaugural meeting of the World Trade Organisation in Singapore, the official said.

Clinton was expected to press for language in the summit declaration expressing support for zero tariffs on a broad range of information technology equipment by the year 2000, but with some flexibility in its implementation.
Clinton asked Hashimoto to help him promote the plan with the other leaders after APEC foreign and trade ministers at their annual meeting this weekend gave only muted support for the plan.

"I would like to ask for your cooperation over the wording of the ITA in the summit declaration," a Japanese foreign ministry spokesman quoted Clinton as telling Hashimoto after a meeting between the two Sunday.
Japan, as a major player in the computer market, supports the U.S. push for free trade in information technology.

Philippine Foreign Affairs Undersecretary Rodolfo Severino told a news briefing that Clinton and President Fidel Ramos also discussed the Information Technology Agreement at their bilateral meeting on the summit's sidelines. Ramos is chairing the main APEC event.
"Discussions are going on and it's at rather a sensitive stage," Severino said.
"Now things are going on so an acceptable formulation can be included in the leaders' statement," he said.

The ministers said in the statement they "endorsed the efforts at WTO to conclude an information technology agreement by the Singapore Ministerial Conference and urged all other members of the WTO to work toward that end."
The United States says the information technology business is worth at least $1 trillion a year, with 80 percent of that in the booming Asia-Pacific region.
